newsitem.title: CHINA: China mineral law to curb chaos, ease investment.
newsitem.headline: China mineral law to curb chaos, ease investment.

text.p: Beijing's new-look minerals law is an important step in developing China's mining industry and boosting foreign exploitation of the country's rich mineral resources, officials and industry experts said on Tuesday.

Amendments to the law that take effect on January 1, 1997, would end confusion over the ownership of China's underground treasures by affirming that it all belongs to the state, said Minister of Geological and Mineral Resources Song Ruixiang.
The changes would also end a ban on the sale of prospecting and mining rights, and legislate a role for foreign investors in the industry, Song told a Beijing news conference.
"(The amendments) assure the legal status of foreign investors' exploration and exploitation of mineral resources, and permit the creation of specific rules to regulate foreign investment," he said.

Industry analysts say China urgently needs foreign funding to develop its mining industry, long plagued by shortages of capital and by loose management of tens of thousands of small scale and inefficient local mine operators.

If remote regions of resource-rich central and western China implemented the new law properly, they would be able to attract more foreign investment, Jiang Chengsong, director of the minerals ministry's General Office, told the news conference.
"This will end the problem of an incomplete law creating a chaotic situation," Jiang said.
China has already banned gold mining in a remote nature reserve in its far west because of a flood of illegal small prospectors, many digging by hand and wasting much of China's mineral resources.

The amendments were part of a necessary change in approach to the minerals sector, which had long permitted foreign involvement on an ad-hoc basis without clear legal guidance, said a minerals analyst at a Western company in Beijing.

"The Chinese were petrified of joint-venture mining because it was a reminder of past exploitation...it was an echo of colonialism where China's resources would be mined and exported by foreign firms," said the analyst, who declined to be named.
"In the meantime they have wasted a lot of precious resources," she said.

Small mines and processing enterprises were often unable to extract secondary minerals from their ore, losing out on a crucial revenue source and creating huge waste, said a senior official at a major state-run metals firm.
"The important part of the new law is first to bring the domestic industry under control, not to attract foreign investment," said the official, who declined to be identified.

"In some places, small-scale mining by individuals is fairly common, and tungsten and rare earth in particular are chaotically mined," he said. "Under these kinds of conditions, how could foreign businessmen come to invest?"

China's State Council, or cabinet, was preparing detailed regulations to govern foreign investment and the transfer of mining rights, said Wu Fuzhao, a member of the law committee of the National People's Congress, or parliament.
Speculation in exploitation or exploration rights would be banned, Wu told the news conference.
The new-look minerals law was a major boost to China's army of miners in their quest to wrest prosperity from the earth, said the metals enterprise official.
"This will help cut the waste in resources," he said. "It's important...because mineral resources can be mined only once and if they are lost, they are gone forever."
